item.title: Remodeling Innovation Is Helping Affordable Housing With Its Deferred Maintenance Problem
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Affordable housing carries a repair backlog measured in the hundreds of thousands of dollars per unit, and prefabricated interior systems are making those renovations cheaper to execute.

The post Remodeling Innovation Is Helping Affordable Housing With Its Deferred Maintenance Problem appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
The country’s affordable housing stock is old and getting older. More than half of active Section 9 public housing units were built before 1975, and the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit program is approaching 40 years old, with portfolios that have grown and aged along with it. Decades of underinvestment have left units in disrepair, and the cost of catching up has climbed steeply as the delay has lengthened. The baseline cost of preserving the nation’s 899,047 public housing units now stands at $169.1 billion, an average of $188,090 per unit with another $3,597 per unit accruing annually as building systems age, according to a 2026 assessment from the 10 Year Roadmap for Public Housing Sustainability and the Public and Affordable Housing Research Corporation. The last comparable federal estimate, from 2010, came to $26 billion.

Candice Delamarre, co-founder of Kit Switch, came at the problem by asking why owners with capital available were still not getting the work done. The answer she kept finding had to do with coordination rather than money. “We saw that so many buildings were not getting renovated and upgraded,” she said. “A big reason for that is that remodels usually have five to eight trades that all need to work in coordination.” Scheduling that many subcontractors into an occupied building, in sequence, with each one’s delay cascading into the next, is expensive in ways that do not show up cleanly in a bid.

Kit Switch, which is organized as a public benefit corporation, sells a packaged approach to renovating buildings that begins with the kitchen. Its components are sized to move into existing buildings without demolition to get them into place. The kitchen product breaks into three pieces covering cooking, cleaning, and storage, and installs on site in less than a day, compared with the four to five days of labor a conventional install requires. Plug-and-play electrical and plumbing connections are consolidated inside the kits, which cuts much of the drywall and trade work the job would otherwise generate.

The kits also limit how much drywall has to be opened, which matters in older buildings that frequently contain lead paint and asbestos. Any scope that opens a wall assembly can trigger abatement protocols that add cost and time, so the company designed its cabinets to avoid that step where possible. “Cutting into a wall is dirty, time-consuming, and could put people in contact with contamination, so we created a back panel for our cabinets that can rerun electrical and create a flat structure,” Delamarre said.

The system also lets residents stay in their homes during the work. For affordable housing owners, relocation carries a particular cost, since a subsidized tenant often has to be placed in a market-rate unit while the renovation happens, with the owner covering the difference out of the project budget. “Occupied rehab is a huge advantage for affordable housing. It prevents the owner from needing to put the tenants in market rate housing, which comes at a loss,” Delamarre said. “Tenants also often push back against relocation.” Residents with children in local schools or medical care nearby have reasons to resist a move that have nothing to do with the renovation itself.

Delamarre uses the phrase “dignified housing” to describe what gets lost when those renovations do not happen. Subsidized rent does not mean a resident should have to live with a broken kitchen or a bathroom that has not been updated in four decades.

Switching to a new construction technique depends on contractors agreeing to work differently, which has defeated plenty of construction innovation before. Delamarre has invested heavily in those relationships, in part because older buildings often bring surprises that slow crews down and lead to repeated change orders. “Building trust with contractors is so important and takes time,” she said. “We also have to spend a lot of time educating contractors about exactly what comes in the kit and what needs to be done beforehand.” A more straightforward path to a remodel benefits both the owner and the contractors involved.

What Delamarre has encountered in those conversations runs against the industry’s assumptions about trade resistance. “There are always worries about how the trades are going to receive innovation, that it won’t be welcome,” she said. “We see the opposite. Contractors are excited to see someone that has made things easier for them.”

Part of that reception has to do with what contractors are normally handed on affordable projects. Budgets push toward the cheapest available cabinets, fixtures, and appliances, which tend to be harder to install, more prone to failure, and more likely to generate a callback. A crew that has spent years working with low-grade materials on tight margins has reason to welcome a system that goes in faster and comes back less often.

Whether prefabricated interiors can reach the volume needed to make a dent in the preservation backlog remains an open question. The approach does give owners a way to update older units with less disruption and less labor, and as the supply of skilled tradespeople tightens, we are likely to see more methods aimed at the same problem.

The post Remodeling Innovation Is Helping Affordable Housing With Its Deferred Maintenance Problem appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Hotel Collapse May Erase Even AAA-Rated CMBS Bonds
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Two Portland Hilton hotels face an 83% value drop, threatening total loss for all CMBS bondholders including AAA-rated tranches.

The post Hotel Collapse May Erase Even AAA-Rated CMBS Bonds appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Two Hilton-branded hotels in Portland, the Hilton Portland Downtown and the Duniway Portland, are headed for a complete CMBS wipeout after their combined appraised value dropped to $58 million from $340.3 million in 2019. Brookfield Asset Management affiliates own the 782-room properties, which carry $240 million in debt packaged into a single-asset, single-borrower CMBS in 2019. Brookfield defaulted in 2020, and foreclosure transferred ownership to the CMBS trust in 2023. After accounting for $53 million in servicer advances and other costs, bondholders in every tranche, including those once rated AAA, face total loss.

No CMBS deal has wiped out top-rated tranches since the financial crisis, though a handful came close. Situs AMC, the special servicer, plans minor property improvements and aims to wait for a Portland hospitality rebound in 2027 or 2028. Shlomo Chopp of Case Equity Partners said bondholders often delay distressed sales to avoid crystallizing losses, but rising interest rates and mounting distressed inventory make delay increasingly costly. Hotel occupancy in Portland’s central business district fell to 62.9% in October from 79.5% in October 2019, and revenue per available room dropped 31% over the same period.

Portland’s downtown real estate has repriced sharply since the pandemic. The city’s tallest office tower sold in 2023 for $45 million, an 87% discount from its prior sale, and roughly 40% of downtown offices sit vacant. A Portland Marriott acquired in 2013 for $82.7 million sold earlier this year for $30 million, the first hotel trade in the city since Covid. Three comparable hotel properties are in escrow to close by year-end, according to servicer notes.

More than $36 billion in single-asset, single-borrower CMBS reaches final maturity in 2027, over three times the volume due this year, according to Barclays. Higher interest rates mean properties appraised at pre-Covid values can no longer support the debt levels buyers and sellers once relied on. Portland’s struggles—Covid shutdowns, months of protests, surging homelessness, and new taxes that lifted rates for high earners to among the nation’s highest—cost the region 8,800 jobs last year and continue to suppress property values as mortgages mature.

Bloomberg
Unprecedented CMBS Debt Wipeout Is Coming for Two Hilton Hotels

The post Hotel Collapse May Erase Even AAA-Rated CMBS Bonds appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: 24 Percent Default Interest Rates Return as Distressed Debt Funds Test Limits
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Brooklyn judge blocks Maverick from foreclosing on Red Hook property over one-day-late payment as distressed lender imposes 24 percent default interest.

The post 24 Percent Default Interest Rates Return as Distressed Debt Funds Test Limits appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
A Brooklyn judge blocked Maverick Real Estate Partners from foreclosing on a Red Hook industrial property after the lender declared a $45 million loan in default over a payment made one day late. David Brecher of FM Capital wired his August payment to Maverick hours after the August 11 deadline, but Brecher argued the default notice did not take effect until after Maverick received the funds. Kings County Justice Genine Edwards issued a temporary order preventing Maverick from accelerating the $41.7 million remaining balance, foreclosing or transferring the property at 160 and 168 Van Brunt Street.

Maverick purchased the loan in early 2024 after Signature Bank collapsed and its portfolio went up for sale. Brecher had converted the former ship engine facility into mixed-use space with more than $15 million in improvements, landing tenants including an NYU hospital center and Tesla’s first New York location. Maverick responded to the late payment by demanding immediate repayment of the full balance and imposing 24 percent default interest. Maverick also cited a missed certified rent roll and alleged failures to maintain a 70 percent loan-to-value ratio and 6.5 percent debt yield as reasons it could not extend the loan.

Maverick, led by Ted Martell and David Aviram, has built a business buying distressed commercial loans and enforcing strict default provisions. In 2024 the firm purchased $247 million in Signature Bank loans from Blackstone secured by properties in Manhattan, Brooklyn and Queens. Borrowers have accused Maverick in multiple lawsuits of manufacturing defaults over minor issues such as unpaid utility bills, though the company maintains it operates within loan terms. Maverick foreclosed on Chetrit Group’s West 34th Street hotel project in 2023 and has expanded from loans in the $1 million to $10 million range to larger commercial deals.

item.title: Robotics Could Shrink the Factory Footprint Just as It Returns to the U.S.
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Capital will underwrite power, not rent

The post Robotics Could Shrink the Factory Footprint Just as It Returns to the U.S. appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
1 day 1 hr agoNov. 23, 2026 3:15 pm

Industrial real estate gets discussed as one asset class, but the buildings inside it are starting to answer to different physics. Logistics demand is organized around volume, throughput, and proximity to population. Manufacturing demand is organized around power, process control, and tolerances. Automation is widening that separation, since companies moving AI and robotics from pilots into production are finding that the same efficiency gains that compress time also compress the floor area required to produce it. The sector returning to the US may end up needing less space than the one that left.

Manufacturing is still a small slice of a market JLL measures at roughly 16.2 billion square feet of US inventory. Space requirements tied to manufacturing grew from about 26 million square feet in 2020 to 124 million in 2024 and were projected to pass 135 million last year, which works out to roughly 19 percent of overall industrial requirements. JLL expects that to reach 30 percent by 2028. CBRE recorded manufacturing-based leasing up 35 to 45 percent in some regions during 2025, the first year it cleared single digits as a share of total leasing. NAIOP has projected reshoring could add more than 10 percent to the domestic manufacturing base over the next decade, around 500 million square feet, which against 16.2 billion comes to about three percent of existing stock.

Logistics still fills the buildings. Third-quarter leasing hit 202.6 million square feet nationally, the strongest quarter since 2022, driven heavily by data center suppliers and power infrastructure. Manufacturing is the demand story that dominates the policy conversation and logistics is the one that shows up in absorption.

What is actually coming back is not general assembly. JLL counted more than 500 post-IRA onshoring projects across semiconductors, life sciences, batteries, aerospace, and advanced materials. Micron has committed $200 billion across Idaho and New York. Texas Instruments is building an $11 billion fab in Lehi, Utah. Amkor raised its Peoria investment from $2 billion to $7 billion for 750,000 square feet of cleanroom. Eli Lilly announced $27 billion for domestic production. Manufacturing construction has been running above $223 billion annualized, more than double where it sat in February 2020.

These facilities are expensive per square foot rather than large in square feet. Semiconductor plants can require 200 megawatts at opening and scale toward 1,200 at full buildout, which puts the utility ahead of the highway interchange in any site selection conversation. Cleanroom classification, vibration isolation, water treatment, redundant power, and network latency all rank above clear height and dock door count. A fab occupying a fraction of a bulk distribution center’s footprint can carry construction costs an order of magnitude higher.

Robotics should push that footprint down further as it arrives. Around 80 percent of US factories currently run without any automation at all, which says more about how much room there is to deploy than about the technology. Physical AI has started letting robots learn by demonstration rather than written code, cutting the engineering cost of a first installation, and lighter collaborative hardware released this year is built specifically for tight spaces and buildings that cannot handle the floor loading or safety caging older industrial arms demand. BCG estimates agentic AI and advanced robotics could make factories roughly 2.5 times more productive. Same output, less floor, fewer people moving through it, and more electricity.

Plenty of projects still run enormous. Rivian’s Georgia campus covers about 9 million square feet for 400,000 vehicles a year, which is the old model at full scale, and vehicle assembly, battery production, and anything involving large physical objects will keep needing room. The point is not that factories are shrinking across the board. It is that the median advanced manufacturing requirement and the median logistics requirement have stopped resembling each other, and averaging the two produces a number that describes neither.

That makes this the second line running through a market already splitting along building age and quality, where Class A space over a million square feet has tightened to 5.4 percent vacancy while older inventory bleeds occupancy. Developers who spent a decade building speculative bulk warehouse have a product suited to one half of the demand. We would expect capital chasing manufacturing exposure to start behaving more like infrastructure investing, underwritten against interconnection queues and tenant process requirements rather than rent per square foot, which is not the business most industrial developers are in today.

The post Robotics Could Shrink the Factory Footprint Just as It Returns to the U.S. appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Leasing Momentum and Deep Sale Discounts Redefine Office Investment in 2027
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Office buildings sell at deep discounts despite improving leasing fundamentals, with nontraditional buyers and adaptive reuse poised to reshape the sector in 2027.

The post Leasing Momentum and Deep Sale Discounts Redefine Office Investment in 2027 appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Office buildings continue to sell at steep discounts even as leasing fundamentals improve. Yardi Matrix reported in September that 48% of urban office deals and 42% of suburban transactions with comparable prior sales closed below their previous purchase prices since 2024. Central business districts saw the sharpest declines, with 73% of deals done at a discount. Doug Ressler, manager of business intelligence at Yardi Matrix, expects forced sales from maturing loans to peak in 2027, with discounts persisting for older assets while premium properties stabilize.

Scott Homa, head of office research at Jones Lang LaSalle, said vacancy rates are declining and supply-demand conditions favor landlords, but capital valuations remain depressed by financing costs. High interest rates following years of near-zero borrowing costs have created downward pressure on asset values independent of operating performance. Homa sees more upside than downside in 2027 if macroeconomic conditions allow interest rate cuts, which would let leasing fundamentals drive pricing. Political factors and potential energy price declines could ease inflationary pressure and trigger monetary policy changes.

Nontraditional buyers are entering the market in greater numbers, including high-net-worth individuals, owner-occupants, and hedge funds able to deploy low-leverage capital. Universities in urban cores are acquiring discounted administrative space previously out of reach at peak pricing. Ressler noted that depreciated values may finally make adaptive reuse projects economically viable after years of limited activity. Cash-rich buyers and opportunistic investors are repositioning tired buildings with fresh approaches that conventional owners had not pursued.

The Business Journals
Offices Are Still Selling at a Discount. Here's What That Means for 2027.

item.title: Luxury Estate Builders in California Use ADU Laws to Expand Compounds
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Atherton homeowners are using California ADU laws to build pool houses and gyms that count toward state affordable housing mandates.

The post Luxury Estate Builders in California Use ADU Laws to Expand Compounds appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Venture capitalist Samir Kaul added a 952-square-foot pool house to his Atherton, California compound by classifying it as an accessory dwelling unit. The structure includes a breezeway for table tennis, an outdoor shower, a living plant roof and a bar, but no bedroom. After Atherton’s planning department requested changes, the Kauls added a “sleeping area,” renamed the project from “Pool House” to “Detached ADU,” and reported $0 rent. The town approved the project and reported it to the state’s housing authority as very low-income housing.

Bloomberg identified 46 compounds in Atherton—two or more adjacent parcels owned by the same person or family. At least three compounds received permits for ADUs marked as very low-income housing because owners reported charging no rent. Plans for one compound’s low-income ADU show a golf simulator in the basement. Marc Andreessen and his wife have assembled five lots into a 12.70-acre estate; the family spent more than $100 million on land alone. Venture capitalist Ryan Sweeney’s family razed a house to build a baseball diamond on one lot and added an ADU on another.

California mandated that Atherton make way for 348 housing units over eight years, including 148 for low and very low-income people. The town approved more than 100 ADUs from 2023 through 2025 to meet state requirements. Vice mayor Rick DeGolia estimates that 2% of ADUs in Atherton are available on the open market; most are used to house family members or remain unoccupied. HIP Housing, a nonprofit home-sharing program, made two matches in Atherton over three years, while 40 people remain on a waitlist seeking housing in the town.

Atherton’s approach reflects a gap between state housing mandates and their local implementation. California requires every municipality to facilitate new housing, but provides little scrutiny over how ADUs are occupied or priced. The state certified Atherton’s housing plan, which relies heavily on ADUs, even as most serve as amenities for compound owners rather than rental housing. A developer submitted plans this summer for 30 townhomes on a one-acre parcel near transit, which would be Atherton’s first multifamily project and could bypass typical resident review periods under new state transit-oriented development laws.

Where Pool Houses Count as Affordable Housing

item.title: Curtailment Events Are Pushing Properties Toward Smarter Microgrids
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
As PJM demand and capacity costs surge, commercial buildings are using microgrids, demand response, and smart load controls to boost grid resilience.

The post Curtailment Events Are Pushing Properties Toward Smarter Microgrids appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
A record heat wave hit the Mid-Atlantic in July, and PJM Interconnection, the grid operator responsible for electricity across 13 states from Illinois to New Jersey and roughly 67 million people, watched regional demand climb to 168,158 megawatts, past a record that had stood for two decades. Grid operators needed capacity from wherever they could find it.

One source was a federal research campus in suburban Maryland. The General Services Administration’s White Oak campus, which hosts an FDA research facility, disconnected from the grid, kept its operations running on its own generation, and sent the surplus back. Across three days it exported more than 58,000 kilowatt-hours, enough to power 600 homes, and at peak supplied 2.5 megawatts, roughly ten times what it normally contributes.

Those three days were unusual in scale rather than in kind. By early September the campus had entered island mode 48 times during 2026, running independently for a combined 54 hours.

Greg Turner, Chief Solutions Engineering Officer at Honeywell Technologies, was among the people who designed that system, and he is direct that White Oak was built for a specific set of circumstances rather than as a general template. The campus sits at the end of a utility feeder, and the research happening inside it cannot tolerate an interruption. “Everyone has a different reason for creating a microgrid, it’s important to know yours up front,” he said. “This project was at the far end of an electrical grid so they knew they were at risk of disruption and that they needed to be able to island their property in case of a power outage.”

Turner also acknowledges that a conventional demand response setup would have been considerably simpler to build. Islanding a campus means synchronizing generation, managing critical loads during the transition, and maintaining power quality without the grid as a reference. Most properties do not need that and should not pay for it.

What is changing is the calculation for everyone else. Curtailment calls have become more frequent and more consequential as capacity markets tighten, and the financial stakes attached to responding well have grown considerably. PJM’s 2026/2027 capacity auction cleared at the FERC-approved ceiling of $329.17 per megawatt-day, the highest in the market’s history and a 22 percent increase over a prior year that had itself jumped more than 800 percent. Total emergency demand response revenue in PJM rose 464 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared to the same period a year earlier.

Those costs land on commercial ratepayers whether they participate or not, adding roughly two to four cents per kilowatt-hour to all-in electricity costs across the PJM footprint starting in June. Properties that enroll and fail to perform face a different problem, since emergency programs can impose clawbacks that exceed the capacity payments a facility received, and some interruptible tariffs carry penalties running several times the firm demand rate.

The upside has grown along with the risk, and it compares favorably to the other way buildings have tried to monetize on-site generation. Net metering compensation has been cut repeatedly as states have moved toward avoided-cost rates, which has made exporting solar to the grid a much weaker proposition than it was a decade ago. Turner sees curtailment programs as the better market. “Net metering is not a very attractive proposition,” he said. “Selling it back under a curtailment program is much more attractive, the utility is looking to buy at really high prices and so they are much more willing to pay a market rate.” Enrolled facilities in PJM can earn somewhere around $120,000 per megawatt annually in capacity payments before any energy revenue.

Most properties cannot generate their way to that position, which is where the engineering problem starts. “Most people are not able to build a microgrid big enough to power the entire campus,” Turner said. “So the challenge is to figure out how to get your load down to a place where onsite generation can help enough to make a difference.” A building with 400 kilowatts of generation and a two megawatt load has to shed well over a megawatt before the generation matters, and it has to do that without shutting down the business inside.

Doing it well requires the power management system and the building management system to coordinate on a rotation, shedding and restoring loads in a sequence that keeps the total under target while spreading the disruption. That is a harder control problem than it sounds, and it runs on software that most buildings do not have, operated by engineers who understand both the electrical side and the mechanical side.

It also requires hardware in places nobody thought to put it. “Some buildings will need to put in control inputs for things they never thought they needed to turn off,” Turner said. “Commercial refrigeration, even though it can never get turned off, might need to get adjusted to change the temperature a bit to reduce the use of the chilling systems.” Work through the Department of Energy’s Better Buildings program has shown that accepting a two-degree drift in commercial refrigeration across a four-hour event can shed 450 kilowatts at a single facility, which is meaningful capacity from equipment that stays running the entire time.

Rising rates are pulling more properties toward this. Capacity costs are flowing into bills across most major markets, data center load growth is tightening reserve margins faster than new generation can be built, and the spread between a managed peak and an unmanaged one keeps widening. Some industrial parks have started marketing energy price stability as an amenity, pitching tenants on predictability rather than on rate alone.

White Oak is a more elaborate installation than most properties will ever justify, built for a campus with unusual requirements and financed through a federal contracting mechanism that commercial owners cannot access. What it demonstrates is narrower and more portable than the full system, which is that a property able to control its own load and generation has options during a grid event that a property without those capabilities does not.

item.title: UK Looks to Abolish Leasehold System That Kept Landlords as Building Owners
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Britain's new legislation bans leasehold flats by 2031, caps ground rents, and shifts ownership to commonhold—ending centuries of tenant control by landlords.

The post UK Looks to Abolish Leasehold System That Kept Landlords as Building Owners appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Britain’s Labour government introduced legislation on November 19 to dismantle the centuries-old leasehold property system, which currently allows buyers of apartments to purchase only the right to occupy a unit for a fixed term—not the land beneath it. The Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill would ban the sale of most new leasehold flats by 2031 and make “commonhold” the default ownership structure, allowing residents to own their apartments outright and collectively manage communal areas. For existing leases, the bill caps ground rents at £250 annually for 40 years before reducing them to nominal amounts. The changes take effect in 2029, with the ground rent cap arriving in 2028 after Royal Assent.

Leasehold ownership, which dates to the Norman invasion and spread widely after the 1950s as apartment construction accelerated, has long drawn criticism for giving freeholders control over building alterations, maintenance charges, and ground rents. Property developers in recent years have extracted higher ground rents, and leaseholders have faced uncapped fees for repairs and upgrades—especially in newer apartment blocks. The 2017 Grenfell Tower fire, which killed 72 residents and exposed substandard cladding, left many leaseholders unable to sell their homes or liable for expensive safety upgrades. The Labour government faces pressure to improve conditions for homeowners squeezed by rising interest rates since the pandemic.

Nearly 80% of real estate agents report that leasehold properties with escalating ground rents are difficult to sell, according to a Propertymark survey, and increased awareness of leasehold issues has led buyers to negotiate harder on price. The ground rent cap is expected to raise leasehold property values and lower freehold prices where leaseholders currently pay significant annual sums. Campaigners have welcomed the bill but raised concerns about existing buildings, which are not required to convert to commonhold—potentially making older leasehold flats less attractive. Liam Spender of the Leaseholder Action campaign group said the cap “sounds the death knell for leasehold in England and Wales” by making freehold purchases cheaper for existing leaseholders.

Why England’s Centuries-Old Leasehold Property System Is Ending

item.title: Downtown Churches Enter the Development Game as Property Values Surge
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Nashville churches with property worth tens of millions explore sales as congregations weigh mission priorities against booming real estate values.

The post Downtown Churches Enter the Development Game as Property Values Surge appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
First Evangelical Lutheran Church and Watson Grove Baptist Church in Nashville have hired Foundry Commercial’s Mission Property Group to market their properties after years of internal deliberation. First Lutheran’s two downtown parking lots, purchased for $2.2 million between 2000 and 2012, now carry an appraised value exceeding $28 million. Watson Grove’s 1.51-acre Edgehill site, acquired for $2,000 in 1955, is now valued at $14.5 million. Both congregations must vote to approve any transaction, and both require that deals align with their mission objectives beyond financial returns.

Religious organizations own property worth $4.5 billion across Davidson County, Tennessee—roughly 4,250 acres or 1.5 percent of the county’s parceled land. First Lutheran is requiring any buyer to include 100 parking spaces reserved for church use in development plans. Watson Grove, which grew from 300 to 3,000 members between 2012 and 2020, explored building a $120 million mixed-use project before turning to a potential sale or ground lease. Pastor John Faison said any deal must enable the church to fulfill its mission, or the congregation will reject it.

Commercial developers and homebuilders have replaced other churches as the primary buyers of religious properties, particularly in markets where developable land has grown scarce. Foundry’s Mission Property Group has facilitated sales of more than 3,000 churches nationwide. The firm’s Matt Messier said congregational approval processes often stretch three to five years due to emotional attachment to buildings that have hosted generations of family events. Pastor Travis Meier said the scale of interest in First Lutheran’s lots—from local investors to global hotel conglomerates—far exceeded expectations for a property that once served simply as income-generating parking.

As Neighborhoods Transform, Church Congregations Face Weighty and Lucrative Real Estate Choices

item.title: How to Get Real Estate Teams Behind an AI Rollout
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Studio
item.description:
Real estate firms are deploying AI faster than they are preparing the people who will use it. JLL's Reeves Davis explains why employee buy-in drives the return.

The post How to Get Real Estate Teams Behind an AI Rollout appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Real estate organizations have moved on AI quickly, and in many cases the decision to deploy has run well ahead of any conversation with the people who will actually use the tools. Software gets selected, a rollout date gets set, and training arrives as a thirty-minute session the week before launch. The staff expected to change how they work find out what is happening when it is already happening.

Adoption suffers when that happens, and so does the return the investment was supposed to generate. AI in real estate operations is mostly justified on productivity, and productivity gains require people to use the tools willingly and well. A platform that sits unused, or gets worked around, produces none of it. Thoughtfully integrating AI in a real estate company’s current tech stack is the key to maximizing the ROI of AI investment.

JLL has a longstanding framework for thinking about where cost sits in an organization, and Reeves Davis, President of Technology Services at JLL, applies it to this problem. The 3-30-300 rule holds that a company spends roughly $3 per square foot annually on utilities, $30 on rent, and $300 on payroll. Because payroll is an order of magnitude larger than rent, a 10 percent productivity gain returns about $30 per square foot, which covers the entire rent line on its own.

That same arithmetic governs AI investment, and capturing the productivity piece depends on how people experience the change. “You have to make sure people feel safe and supported,” Davis said. “If I can get even slightly better productivity, it could save the company way more than any other improvement that tech can bring on its own.”

A well-received rollout delivers more than the productivity gain. “We think about introducing productivity improvements as a way to copy the best employees in a systematized way,” Davis said. “Now the onboarding process is much faster and you are enabling people with a very standardized toolset.” Encoding a process into a tool makes it available to everyone rather than to whoever learned it from the person who knew it best.

Deployment is also not the end of the work. Usage data tells an organization whether the tools are being used at all, and Davis sees a second benefit in tracking it. “Tracking the usage of tools is critical, it shows people that you care enough to track it and take the way they interact with a product into consideration,” he said. “People want to think they are working for a company that is trying to make their job better.”

What comes back from that monitoring feeds the next round of decisions. The number of plausible AI projects always exceeds the capacity to pursue them, and Davis describes choosing among them as a capability organizations have to develop rather than something they can plan for in advance. “There will never be enough time and money to attack every idea up front so companies have to build the muscle of assessing which tech to work on,” he said.

This work is going to continue for years rather than quarters. The tools will keep changing, the workflows built around them will keep getting rebuilt, and organizations will be making these decisions repeatedly rather than once. Each round of that cycle depends on whether the last one left people more willing to engage or less.

That makes the early rollouts worth getting right for reasons beyond their individual returns. A deployment that staff experienced as something done to them makes the next one harder, because people arrive skeptical and participate minimally. One that visibly improved their work produces the opposite, and the organization gets better feedback, faster adoption, and a clearer sense of what to build next. The productivity gains that justify AI investment in the first place come from people choosing to use these tools rather than tolerating them, which is a different thing to design for than a deployment timeline.
